title: NVTX timeline sampling and L2 backpressure correlation - Feb 2026
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from the NVTX/Nsight Systems profiling runs that looked specifically at L2/backpressure effects and how our CUDA-graph capture + async copy pattern interacts with kernel timelines. This is a working doc — rough observations, screenshots referenced by timestamp in Nsight session, and a few actionable experiments.

Motivation / symptom:
- Customers observe occasional 2-4x tail latency spikes in multi-tenant Dedicated pools when sequence lengths are skewed.
- Hypothesis: cache/bandwidth backpressure (L2/DRAM) plus cudaGraph capture behavior causes kernel pipeline skew across microbatches and ends up serializing what should be concurrent execution.

Test setup (short):
- Model: gpt-medium-ish config (12B-ish params trimmed for test), FP16, KV cache used across tokens.
- HW: A100-SXM4 40GB, driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.1.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch: feature/async-capture-fix (see PR linked).
- Workload: synthetic traffic with two microbatch shapes: {mb=1, seq=1024} and {mb=8, seq=256} mixed 70/30.
- Instrumentation: NVTX ranges around: encode, kv-lookup, attention-kernel, ffn-kernel, prefix-copy, async-d2h/d2d. Inserted NVTX push/pop at call sites; annotated with request-id and microbatch-id.
- Nsight command (capture): nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --output=nvtx-l2-run-20260220.nsys-rep --duration=45s 

Key observations from Nsight timeline:
1) Repeating waveform: when a long-seq microbatch hits attention-kernel there is a marked ~300-600us drop in concurrent microkernels running on other streams. Timeline shows a burst in L2 read stalls coincident with high L2 transfer bytes.
2) NVTX labels let us correlate a specific request-id to a contiguous span of several kernel launches; between the first and last kernel the SM_ACTIVE fraction drops for other work.
3) CUDA graph capture windows coincide with graph replays that requeue a tight bundle of kernels on the same stream. When the captured graph includes an async D2D prefetch we see the prefetch occupying copy engine and causing small stalls on kernels that expect pinned copy completion ordering.
4) L2 utilization counters: sustained L2 read bandwidth spikes (measured via nsight counters) reached ~85-92% of peak for ~1.2ms windows on long sequence microbatches. Those windows line up with increased warp_stalls due to memory.
5) Microbatch size interaction: mb=8, seq=256 runs more kernels but spreads memory pressure; mb=1, seq=1024 tends to create longer contiguous DRAM bursts and higher instantaneous L2 pressure.

Deep-dive trace snippets (timestamps refer to nsys rep around 00:00:12 - 00:00:14):
- 00:00:12.130 NVTX: attention-kernel(req=2845, mb=1) -> attention-kernel launches set of kernels on stream 2.
- 00:00:12.145 Counters show L2_READ_BYTES high and L2_WRITE_BYTES modest.
- 00:00:12.165 Other streams (stream 5/7) show kernel queuing and increased queue-time before launch (~180-240us).
- 00:00:12.420 NVTX: async-prefetch(d2d) replayed inside cudaGraph on stream 2; memcpy occupies copy engine then a short gap; kernel on stream 5 pushes but waits (queueing grows to ~350us).

Hypothesis refinement:
- Not a pure SM occupancy shortage. SM_ACTIVE% can be high, but memory subsystem (L2 + DRAM) is the bottleneck. Long contiguous token sequences create heavy L2 read bursts that backpressure subsequent kernels via global memory pipeline and L2 contention.
- CudaGraph capture of prefetch + kernels on the same stream amplifies serialization because graph replay reissues a tight sequence that doesn't yield or allow overlapping copy engine work effectively.

Immediate mitigations tested (and observed effects):
- Break captured graphs: capturing smaller subgraphs for KV prefetch separately from compute kernels reduced the observed queue-time for concurrent kernels by ~60% in our synthetic run. Tradeoff: slightly higher kernel launch overhead (+20us per microbatch).
- Introduce small scheduler yield in runtime (cudaStreamQuery or cudaLaunchHostFunc with tiny sleep) after large-copy operations—adds ~50us latency to long-seq requests but reduces tail spikes by ~40%.
- Change stream priorities: giving compute streams higher priority than copy streams reduced observed kernel queueing but caused copy engine saturation for prefetch-heavy cases. Mixed results.

Profiling commands / counters we used (notes for replication):
- nsight counters used: sm__cycles_active.avg.pct, lts__t_sectors_pipe_utilization.avg.pct, lts__throughput.avg.pct, dram__throughput.avg.pct, warp__executed_unresolved_hazards_perc
- nsys export to CSV then jq filter on nvtx ranges to correlate request ids. Quick command: nsys export --output nvtx-l2-run-20260220.csv nvtx-l2-run-20260220.nsys-rep && csvgrep -c "Nvtx Range" -m "attention-kernel" nvtx-l2-run-20260220.csv | head

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
1) Disable capturing prefetch copies and split them into a separate graph or perform prefetch via explicit async memcpy on dedicated stream with careful synchronization (cudaEvent) to avoid graph replay taking copy-engine hostage.
2) Add a configurable micro-yield after large-copy ops in the runtime (opt-in) to allow other streams to make forward progress. Flag likely to be turned on for long-sequence workloads.
3) Expose a "prefer-low-l2-burst" scheduling policy for multi-tenant pools: bias scheduling to interleave short and long sequences, or co-locate long sequences to specific GPUs.

Longer-term experiments to run:
- Kernel pacing: implement a pacing pass that delays kernel launches inside graph replay by a few microseconds to smooth L2 pressure and measure tail-latency impact (open PR planned).
- Quantized-kernel memory pattern analysis: run same trace with int8 kernels to check whether memory bandwidth reduction eliminates the backpressure (good validation for QAT/quant path).
- Persistent-kernel variant: try a persistent attention kernel which maintains higher occupancy but filters memory access pattern to reduce bursts.

Notes / open questions:
- Is the copy engine contention consistent across A100 variants? Need cross-hardware runs (A100 80GB, H100) to rule out PCIe vs NVLink effects.
- Does NUMA on multi-socket hosts (DGX) change behavior: pinned host staging vs D2D prefetch path differences.

Next steps (owners):
- Aisha: open a small feature branch to split prefetch into separate graph + basic scheduling flag (ETA 1 week).
- Daniel: schedule full-suite Nsight capture across A100-80 and H100 (ETA 2 weeks).
- Marta: write a benchmark for mixed-shape microbatch scheduling to quantify tail-latency improvement (ETA 1.5 weeks).

Appendix (quick links / commands):
- extract ranges with python: tools/trace_utils/extract_nvtx_ranges.py nvtx-l2-run-20260220.nsys-rep > ranges.json
- quick NVTX macros used: NVTX_PUSH_FMT("req=%d mb=%d phase=%s", req, mb, phase)
- related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4312

Screenshots / artifacts: see Nsight capture under /mnt/profiles/2026/02/nvtx-l2-run-20260220.nsys-rep and the exported CSV in the same folder.

Rough verdict: L2/backpressure + cudaGraph capture interplay is a credible root cause for observed tail spikes. Short-term mitigation (split prefetch from compute graph) gives measurable wins with an acceptable overhead. Further validation across hardware and quantized kernels required before rolling to prod default.

-- aisha
